Chapter 8: The Mirror of Literature—Women as Reflections, Not Subjects.
There’s this strange kind of double vision that happens when women go searching for themselves in the world of literature. For centuries, the shelves were packed with stories written by men, about men, and—let’s be honest—mostly for men.
When women showed up in those stories, they were usually just reflections. Sometimes a muse, other times a temptress, a saint, or maybe even a sinner—but almost never a fully complex person with her own messy, real life.
Picture someone hoping to find herself in these stories. What does she end up seeing? Women who are beautiful or tragic. Women who spark greatness in the people around them, but rarely get to taste it for themselves. Their lives orbit the men at the center, their dreams and desires shaped by someone else’s imagination.
It’s like gazing into a mirror that distorts your face, only showing what someone else wants to see.
Most folks don’t even notice how much this shapes the way women see themselves. If the only stories out there are told from the outside looking in, it’s tough to imagine what it’s like to truly be the subject of your own story, instead of just the object in someone else’s.
Suddenly, the world starts to feel like a place where women are always being watched, always being judged, but never really in the driver’s seat of their own narrative.
But here’s where things get interesting—a quiet rebellion begins the moment a woman picks up the pen and starts telling her own story. That’s when the mirror starts to crack. The reflection grows more layered, more real.
Sure, the world doesn’t always welcome these new stories with open arms. Critics can be harsh, and some readers might feel uncomfortable. But once that crack appears, the change can’t be stopped.
You start to realize that literature isn’t just a record of what’s already happened. It’s a map of what’s possible. Every time a woman writes herself into the story, the world gets a little bigger. The mirror transforms into a window, and suddenly, new ways of being—new possibilities—come into view.
